body_markdown:
Skin diseases are among the most common health problems worldwide, yet access to specialist care remains deeply unequal. A new international study has highlighted a major shortage of dermatologists across many parts of the world, leaving millions of people without timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.


The research suggests that the problem is particularly serious in poorer countries, where healthcare systems often have very few specialists available to deal with complex skin conditions. While skin problems can affect people almost anywhere, the availability of professional care varies dramatically depending on where someone lives.


## A widespread health problem with limited specialist care


Skin conditions are far more than a cosmetic concern. They include common problems such as acne and scabies, as well as serious diseases, autoimmune disorders and skin cancers. According to figures cited in the report, skin diseases affect approximately one in three people globally. More than 3,000 different skin conditions have been identified.


Despite this enormous burden, specialist resources are unevenly distributed.


Researchers who gathered information from experts in 158 countries found that Europe had approximately six dermatologists for every 100,000 people. In Africa, however, the figure was only around 0.26 dermatologists per 100,000 people.


The difference becomes even more striking when countries are compared according to income. The study found approximately 5.05 dermatologists per 100,000 people in the wealthiest group of countries, compared with only 0.37 per 100,000 in the poorest group.


This means that people living in lower-income countries can face significant difficulties accessing a doctor with specialised training in skin health.


## The human impact of delayed diagnosis


A lack of specialists can have serious consequences for patients, particularly those living with rare or severe conditions.


The report describes the experience of Noel Mudibo, a patient advocate in Nairobi, Kenya, who developed pemphigus vulgaris while he was a student in 2017. The condition caused severe blisters in his mouth and on his legs.


His symptoms became so painful that even brushing his teeth was difficult. He also experienced social stigma, with some people making assumptions about his health and personal circumstances because of his appearance.


His first medical treatment did not solve the problem. A university doctor prescribed antibiotics, but his symptoms continued.


Over several years, Mudibo searched for information about his condition himself, tried traditional medicine and used strong painkillers to cope with the discomfort. Eating became difficult, forcing him to rely on very soft and bland foods.


He eventually received an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment in 2021. Following treatment, he said that he experienced some relief.


His experience illustrates how a shortage of specialist care can affect much more than a patient's physical health. Delays can also contribute to emotional distress, social isolation, financial pressure and uncertainty.


## More than a shortage of doctors


The study's findings suggest that simply increasing the number of dermatologists would not solve every problem.


In some countries, patients also face high treatment costs, limited laboratory facilities and a lack of diagnostic resources. Cultural beliefs and stigma can create additional barriers. In Kenya, for example, some people with rare skin diseases may be told that their symptoms are linked to witchcraft.


These challenges can make it harder for patients to receive an accurate diagnosis and begin treatment quickly.


Expanding specialist services could nevertheless make a significant difference. More dermatologists could improve access to diagnosis, increase awareness of skin diseases and help healthcare systems manage complicated cases.


The researchers also highlighted the potential importance of training other healthcare professionals. General practitioners, nurses and other health workers could receive additional education to recognise and manage common skin conditions, while knowing when patients need specialist treatment.


## Why skin health can be overlooked


One explanation for the shortage is that skin diseases are sometimes regarded as cosmetic problems rather than serious medical conditions.


However, the study's lead investigator, Dr Esther Freeman, argued that this perception does not reflect the reality faced by many patients. Severe skin disease can cause significant disability and can be associated with serious conditions, including advanced skin cancer, severe drug reactions and autoimmune diseases.


The report states that skin conditions are among the top 10 causes of disability worldwide.


This creates an important challenge for healthcare policymakers. When resources are limited, governments must decide how funding is distributed across different areas of healthcare. If skin health is considered less important, specialist services may receive less attention and investment.


## A significant international disparity


The scale of the disparity is illustrated by comparisons between countries with similarly sized populations.


Australia and Niger each have populations of roughly 27 million people, according to the report. However, Australia has more than 600 dermatologists, while Niger has only 18.


The research also found that only one in six countries met the study's benchmark of 5.63 dermatologists per 100,000 people. No countries in Africa or Southeast Asia reached that benchmark.


In some of these regions, the shortage of dermatologists occurs alongside a relatively high burden of skin disease, creating what researchers describe as a particularly difficult combination.


Specialist services, including surgery for skin cancers and dedicated paediatric dermatology care, may be even harder to access.


## What could improve access?


International recognition of skin disease as a public health issue could be an important step.


In 2025, countries agreed at the World Health Organization's annual assembly that skin diseases should be treated as a global health priority. The new research could contribute to efforts to turn that recognition into practical improvements.


Potential measures include investing in specialist training, expanding medical education and improving access to scientific information for healthcare workers.


Training non-specialist healthcare professionals could also help. In areas where dermatologists are scarce, better-trained primary healthcare workers may be able to identify common conditions earlier and refer complicated cases when necessary.


Improving laboratory facilities and reducing financial barriers could also help patients reach the correct diagnosis and treatment.


## Closing the gap


The global shortage of dermatology services demonstrates a wider challenge in healthcare: having a widespread medical condition does not necessarily mean that appropriate treatment is widely available.


For people living with serious or rare skin diseases, the consequences of limited access can be substantial. Delayed diagnosis may prolong pain, increase uncertainty and allow some conditions to become more difficult to manage.


The evidence presented in the study points to the need for greater attention to skin health, particularly in countries where specialist services remain limited.


Better access will likely require more than simply training additional dermatologists. It may also involve strengthening primary healthcare, improving diagnostic facilities, addressing treatment costs and tackling the stigma surrounding visible skin conditions.


Skin disease affects people across the world. Ensuring that people can access appropriate care, regardless of where they live, remains an important global health challenge.

*The Independent* on 16 September 2026.
